strengths: benchmark papers for GNN in this use case are timely
the proposed featurization strategy could be useful for cell-to-cell network analysis but more info needed (see questions)
This manuscript investigates the potential advantages of using GNNs to incorporate cell-cell interactions for analyzing COVID-19 single-cell RNA sequencing data.
The models were applied to the patient state classification problem (healthy, non-ICU, ICU) and evaluated based on clinical data.
The analysis results presented in this study may provide some useful insights for other researchers who investigate similar bioinformatics & medical informatics problems.
Trains five different kinds of GNNs
Labels each edge with scores from 107 pathway-level interactions
Motivation: The problem considered by the authors - i.e., gaining insights on COVID-19 from single-cell data - is clearly significant.
Novelty: The authors' method is, to my knowledge, novel.
weaknesses: clarity on contributions and methodological details (see questions)
Limited technical innovation and lack of biologically/clinically significant novel insights despite bold claims.
The GNNs in this study are simply implemented utilizing existing models in PyTorch, without any additional novel methodological contributions.
Claims of pioneering multiple edge features are not novel; similar efforts have been made in relevant fields for many years.
Prior work (e.g., Zitnik et al. review paper) already discusses use of multiple edge features in network biology, indicating the approach is not new.
Claims of groundbreaking perspective on COVID-19 biology are unsupported by evaluation results; no novel biological or clinical insights are provided.
The authors claim an "innovative" and "pioneering" use of "meticulously constructed" multidimensional edge features, but multidimensional edge features in GNNs have been around for a long time.
The authors claim that these multidimensional edge features make these models very performant, but do not include a single study with a one-dimensional edge features to validate this claim.
In Table 3, standard deviations are typically large and therefore the best performing models are typically not significantly better.

The distribution of severity classes in the UMAPs of Figure 1 do not look visually different from each, which weakens the authors' claims that the MPNN is creating greater cohesion after its conv or pooling layers.

The age-related analysis and its resulting conjecture about model performance on External 2 is weak - there could be many factors contributing to these differences; it would be better to test the hypothesis by, e.g., resampling External 2 to have a similar age distribution then training.
No new biological insights: the claim that the model offers a groundbreaking perspective on the biological complexity of COVID-19 is not supported by the experiments.

No comparisons with GNN baselines: only performance comparisons among different GNN architectures with the authors' graph construction technique are presented, making it impossible to assess performance relative to prior GNN models.
No comparisons with non-GNN baselines: lack of comparison with standard tools like Seurat/scanpy/scVI makes it unclear whether GNNs provide any advantage.
Limited discussion/comparison to previous work: the authors do not discuss previous similar work applying GNNs to single-cell COVID-19 data, hindering assessment of novelty.

Limited details on the graph-building technique: insufficient information about tools such as SpatalkDB and CellchatDB, and excessive discussion of hyperparameter settings that could be moved to the supplement.
